title: The Shop the Campaign Buys: A 10 x 5 Plasma Table and Its Router

chapters.title: The shop the campaign buys
narration: Part of what backing this project pays for is a shop. Not a building: two machines. A plasma table that cuts a whole sheet of steel into the panels of a dome, and a router that cuts the jigs and the wooden panels. This film is what those two machines are, what they make, and what they cost when you build them rather than buy them. Here is the first thing the table makes: one 120 by 60 inch sheet of plate, 40 panels.

chapters.title: One sheet, forty panels
narration: Steel plate comes in sheets ten feet by five, and the table's bed is exactly that size. The torch walks every panel's outline in turn: about 181 feet of cut, roughly 24 minutes of torch time. What comes off the table is the whole shell of a dome, every triangle already the right size, already the right angle at every corner. Nothing is measured with a tape. The machine does the measuring.

chapters.title: How the panels fit
narration: The panels are laid out in 8 strips, each one triangles pointing alternately up and down, the way they tile with nothing between them but the cutting gap. Every panel is slid along until it sits exactly a quarter inch from its neighbour, and then the whole layout is checked part by part. 78 percent of the sheet ends up inside a part. The panels come from the solved dome, so if the geometry changes, the nest changes too.

chapters.title: Almost fits
narration: You can squeeze a slightly bigger shell out of the same sheet by trimming each panel's point and welding a small cap over every vertex. Here the best trim is 0.30 inches off each point, with 16 caps, and it makes the shell 1.4 percent bigger. That is real, and it is small: the strips are already full. Most of the time, cut the panels whole.

chapters.title: Welded up
narration: Welded together, the forty panels make a steel shell 5.2 feet across and 2.6 feet tall. That is 55 seams and 82 feet of weld, about 2.1 hours at a steady hand. In three-millimetre plate the panels weigh 188 pounds; in two-millimetre, 126. Every seam is a butt weld, ground flush where it shows.

chapters.title: What one sheet becomes
narration: Turned over on three short legs, the shell is a bowl holding 237 gallons: a tub. In heavier plate, with a hinged panel for a door and a flue at the top, it is the body of a wood stove. Smaller jobs are a fire bowl, a planter, a seat. A hemisphere does not care which way up it is used, and these are the right first projects while you learn the machine.

chapters.title: What it is not
narration: Here is the number that does not help the pitch. At 2.6 feet tall, a one-sheet shell holds nobody standing up. It is not a storm shelter, and it is not a room. To shelter a person you need a bigger dome, cut from several sheets, and that is the next step.

chapters.title: A dome in plate
narration: The same table cuts the triangles of a building. A three-frequency dome has two panel shapes, and how many sheets it takes depends on whether two strips of its biggest panels fit on a five-foot sheet. At 13 feet across they do: 9 sheets, 69 percent of the steel in parts, about 1,005 pounds in two-millimetre plate. One foot bigger, at 14 feet, they do not, and it takes 16 sheets. Size the dome to the sheet, or cut the big panels in two and weld them.

chapters.title: The table, by the plans' own rules
narration: The table is the Homemade Madness DIY CNC plasma design, and the credit for it is theirs. Their plans are drawn for a two-by-one-metre sheet and give two rules for building it bigger: the frame is two hundred and fifty millimetres longer and wider than the sheet, and the gantry tube is two hundred and fifty-three longer than the cut width. For a ten-by-five-foot sheet that makes a frame 3,298 by 1,774 millimetres. Ours is half again as long as theirs, so we add one change: a leg pair at the middle, so no rail span goes unsupported.

chapters.title: Long rails, joined
narration: No single rail is three metres long at this price, so each side takes three, joined end to end: 10 rails in all, which is 5 of the two-rail kits already bought. Both long sides are driven, so both need rack: 7 half-metre lengths a side, four on the gantry and a spare, 19 in all. Every joint is cut on the tooth and aligned with a spare piece held across it. A joint set by eye makes a machine that cuts a curve.

chapters.title: The number that has to be right
narration: A fifteen-tooth pinion at module one and a half has a 22.5 millimetre pitch diameter, so one turn of the motor moves the axis 70.69 millimetres. With eight microsteps on a two-hundred-step motor, that is 22.64 steps per millimetre. That number goes into the controller before anything is cut. The plans prefer a thirteen-tooth pinion for torque, and say to use what you can find and set the ratio in software.

chapters.title: Motors that fit the pinion
narration: The pinions have a ten-millimetre bore, so the motors must have a ten-millimetre shaft. A NEMA 23 of three newton-metres has one, and fits with no sleeve; a bigger NEMA 34's shaft would not. Two of them on the long axis push a gantry of about 40 kilograms at 6.7 metres per second squared on half their torque, far more than a plasma ever asks for, because a plasma torch pushes on nothing.

chapters.title: Pilot arc and a floating head
narration: The torch rides a floating head that touches the plate to find its height before every cut. Pick a plasma with a pilot-arc start: a high-frequency start puts electrical noise into the control wiring. A torch height controller is left out on purpose. The plans' breakout board cannot run one, and touching off the plate again partway through a long cut does the job for nothing.

chapters.title: What it costs, and what kind of number each is
narration: Built, the plasma table comes to $4,151, and the bill keeps three kinds of price apart. $1,157 is what we actually paid for rack, pinions and rails. $1,654 is current retail listings for the motors, drivers, power supply, Mach3, the plasma cutter and the frame steel. $1,339 is still estimates, labelled as estimates until they are quoted: the slats, the water pan, the plate, the ballscrew and the wiring.

chapters.title: The router head
narration: For $990 more, the same frame becomes a router. The rails, rack, motors and controls stay. The floating head becomes a rigid ballscrew axis with a water-cooled spindle, the slats lift out, and a flat spoilboard goes in. The gantry tube sags 0.03 millimetres under a router's side load, less than the cutter's own wobble. This is the machine that cuts the jigs, the templates and the wooden panels the rest of the method needs.

chapters.title: Budgeted, and built
narration: The campaign budgets $11,800 to buy a plasma table and $14,500 for a router: $26,300 together. Built on one frame, both machines come to $5,141. That difference is real, and so is what it does not include: a bought machine comes with support, a warranty and a phone number. A built one takes weeks of evenings, and its first troubleshooter is its owner. We print both numbers because the choice is real.

chapters.title: What the backing builds
narration: That is what this part of the backing buys: a table that turns a sheet of steel into a dome's panels, a router that turns a sheet of plywood into the jigs that build the wooden ones, and the first things they make. Every number in this film comes from the same code as the book. The table's design is Homemade Madness's; the steel and the sawdust will be ours.

chapters.title: Do the one thing
narration: If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can
carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from
somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field
with a chainsaw.

chapters.title: Follow the experiments
narration: Everything is documented, including the parts that failed.
